extracted.intended_audience: chemical manufacturers, importers, employers, safety professionals, and other stakeholders affected by OSHA's Hazard Communication Standard
extracted.subtask_description: Final rule summary and explanation for updates to OSHA's Hazard Communication Standard (HCS), including incorporation by reference, scope, and revised definitions (e.g., bulk shipment, combustible dust). Intended to guide regulated parties on compliance and interpretation of the revised regulatory text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporation by reference of consensus standards
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA is updating 29 CFR 1910.6 to include the national and international consensus standards listed in the final rule and is finalizing the proposed references to the consensus standards (with one citation correction). Each standard is available for purchase from issuing organizations and inspection at OSHA regional offices or the OSHA Docket Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA will incorporate the specific consensus standards it proposed (rather than updating all references in bulk). Due to copyright, OSHA cannot post consensus standards online; copies are available for purchase or inspection at OSHA offices. Where multiple revisions exist and earlier versions remain relevant, OSHA retains references to older versions in regulatory text to avoid implying retesting or reclassification is necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not require reclassification based on updated test methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Where OSHA has updated consensus standards, OSHA does not intend to require chemicals already classified using an earlier version of a consensus standard to be reclassified and has retained earlier versions of the consensus standards in the text where relevant to avoid suggesting retesting is necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requiring reclassification based on updated test methods could cause unnecessary economic impacts and confusion. OSHA considered but declined adding a DATES provision exempting pre-effective-date classifications, instead retaining explicit references to older versions where relevant (e.g., allowing Rev. 4 or Rev. 6 for certain UN Manual material).

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability and inspection of incorporated standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporated consensus standards are available for purchase from issuing organizations and for inspection at OSHA Regional Offices and the OSHA Docket Office; OSHA will not post copyrighted consensus standards on its website or regulations.gov.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stakeholders seeking to review exact test methods or criteria must obtain or inspect the standards through issuing organizations or OSHA regional/docket offices due to copyright restrictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of the HCS (paragraph (a)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: The purpose is to ensure that the hazards of all chemicals produced or imported are classified, and that information concerning the classified hazards is transmitted to employers and employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA is updating the reference to the GHS to 'Revision 7' and inserts 'primarily' before 'Revision' to reflect that most updates align with Rev.7, with selected provisions aligning with Rev.8 or not relating to the GHS.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and application — nuisance particulates exclusion (paragraph (b)(6)(x))
rubrics_metrics.description: Nuisance particulates are excluded from the HCS scope when the chemical manufacturer or importer can establish they do not pose any physical hazard, health hazard, or other hazards covered under the HCS (i.e., including hazards not otherwise classified (HNOC)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The addition of 'other hazards' clarifies that HNOC must be considered when evaluating nuisance particulates. The provision does not change the longstanding 1994 requirement that nuisance particulates are excluded only if they pose no hazard. OSHA views this as a clarification rather than a substantive change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof for exemption claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The party seeking to claim an exemption (e.g., manufacturer or importer claiming nuisance particulate exclusion) bears the burden of demonstrating that the exemption applies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA relies on judicial precedent (e.g., Triumph Constr. Corp. v. Sec'y of Labor; Harry C. Crooker & Sons v. OSHRC) to support that the burden of proof for an exemption lies with the party claiming it. Comments asserting the change improperly shifts burden were rejected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraph (b)(6)(x) does not establish testing requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraph (b)(6)(x) does not mandate testing or otherwise affect methods of classification under the HCS; the hazard evaluation process for nuisance particulates remains the same as for other chemicals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggestions to change wording to require 'are not classified' (to avoid implying testing) were declined because the provision as written has long been interpreted not to require testing; classification methods remain unchanged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outside-scope issues are not addressed by this rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggestions such as applying the HCS to all chemicals in the United States, pre-approval of labels before use, preventing other agencies or states from setting labeling requirements, or addressing consumer product labeling and pesticidal product SDSs are outside the scope or authority of this rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA will not adopt measures beyond the NPRM's proposals or beyond OSHA's statutory jurisdiction (e.g., preempted areas where other federal agencies have statutory authority). OSHA declines to take requested actions on out-of-scope topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions purpose and placement (paragraph (c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraph (c) provides definitions for terms used throughout the HCS to increase stakeholder comprehension and improve compliance; many definitions align with the GHS, while some are unique to the HCS. Definitions specifically related to individual health and physical hazards appear in Appendices A and B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA proposed modifications to three existing definitions, additions of eight new terms, and deletion of one definition. The Summary and Explanation discusses each definition (alphabetically) and explains finalization decisions and any changes from the NPRM.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finalization of specific definitions (list)
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA is finalizing the definitions of bulk shipment, exposure or exposed, gas, hazardous chemical, immediate outer package, physician or other licensed health care professional (PLHCP), released for shipment, and solid as proposed; eliminating the definition of pyrophoric gas; and finalizing combustible dust, liquid, and physical hazard with changes from the NPRM.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each finalized definition is discussed with reasons for adoption or modification; where OSHA made changes from the NPRM, the Summary and Explanation documents the rationale and responses to comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bulk shipment definition (scope and exclusions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bulk shipment means any hazardous chemical transported where the mode of transportation (vehicle) comprises the immediate container (i.e., contained in tanker truck, rail car, or intermodal container). Intermediate bulk containers (IBCs) and other forms of bulk packaging with intermediate containment are not intended to fall within this definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA intentionally defined 'bulk shipment' differently from DOT's 'bulk packaging' because OSHA's exception in paragraph (f)(5)(ii) is meant to apply only when the transportation mode is itself the immediate container. OSHA declined requests to adopt DOT's broader definition to avoid creating mismatches with HCS labeling intent; coordination with DOT guidance remains possible without identical definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combustible dust definition — intrinsic-property focus and wording changes
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA adopts a definition for combustible dust consistent with GHS Rev.7 but replaces phrases for clarity: removes 'are liable to catch fire' and 'on ignition', replaces 'catch fire' with 'pose a flash-fire hazard', replaces 'explode' with 'explosion hazard', and changes 'particle' to 'particulate'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA's definition is intended to describe intrinsic properties of combustible dusts rather than conditions required for ignition. OSHA declined to include confinement or particle-size criteria (e.g., <500 microns) because those are conditions external to the material and not intrinsic properties. OSHA also declined to adopt the NFPA definition wholesale because the HCS does not require label/SDS preparers to conduct testing; instead, consensus standards and guidance (e.g., NFPA, ISO/IEC) provide test methods and more detailed criteria that classifiers may rely on.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of consensus standards and guidance for classification/testing
rubrics_metrics.description: The HCS provides general definitions for hazards but does not provide the detailed descriptions and test methods required to classify materials; those are provided through guidance materials and consensus standards (e.g., NFPA, ISO/IEC).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classifiers and distributors may continue to rely on consensus standards and industry guidance to determine whether a material meets hazard criteria (for example, using NFPA test methods for combustible dust), and OSHA's definitions are intentionally broad to describe intrinsic hazard properties rather than procedural testing requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmonization approach with international and other consensus standards
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA seeks alignment with the GHS (primarily Rev.7) and where appropriate with other international consensus standards, but will not automatically adopt every external definition or testing requirement if it conflicts with HCS purposes (e.g., test mandates or differing agency jurisdictions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments requesting wholesale adoption of NFPA or DOT definitions were considered; OSHA explained why some departures are appropriate (to avoid implying required testing, to preserve HCS's intrinsic-property definitions, or because DOT's definition would not support specific HCS exceptions). OSHA may consider bulk updating of references to consensus standards in future rulemaking but will only finalize the references proposed in this rule.
